questions.question: Define a GIS, explain the layer principle and overlay analysis, and distinguish spatial data from attribute data with an example.
questions.expected_answer: A Geographical Information System is a computerised system that captures, stores, analyses, manages and displays geographically referenced information — information anchored to a definite position on the earth's surface. The definition has two halves: a GIS is a database, and its data is georeferenced, with every record knowing its location through coordinates, so a list of hospitals becomes geographical information the moment each hospital carries coordinates. The organising idea is the layer: each theme — rivers, roads, settlements, rainfall, population density — is stored as a separate transparent sheet georeferenced to the same coordinate system, so the computer can stack any combination in perfect alignment over the same ground. Combining layers is overlay analysis, which lets the GIS answer WHERE questions no single map could: stacking school-age population, existing schools and roads reveals where a new high school should go; laying buildings over the floodplain layer reveals which farmhouses stand inside the floodline. Every feature carries two kinds of data: spatial data records where it is and its geometry (point, line or area), while attribute data records what it is like — for a hospital, the coordinates are spatial data and the name, number of beds and presence of a trauma unit are attribute data. Selecting a feature opens its attribute table; that link between position and description is the essence of GIS.

questions.question: Name and explain the five components of a GIS, and argue why data is considered the most important component.
questions.expected_answer: HARDWARE: the physical machinery — computers and servers that store and process, screens, printers and plotters, and field capture devices, above all GPS receivers including those in smartphones. SOFTWARE: the programs that capture, store, analyse and display layers, such as QGIS (free) and ArcGIS, with phone mapping applications as everyday examples. DATA: the georeferenced layers themselves, gathered from surveys, GPS capture, digitised maps, administrative records such as the Statistics South Africa census, and remote sensing on a huge scale. PEOPLE: trained operators who capture and clean data, analysts who run and interpret overlays, and decision-makers who act on results — the system computes, humans conclude. PROCEDURES: the working rules that keep the system trustworthy — update schedules, accuracy standards, and records of changes. Data is ranked most important and most expensive because the finest hardware and software produce rubbish from wrong or stale data: an out-of-date school layer will recommend building a school where one already stands, and a GIS never makes old data true, only convincing. The summary: hardware and software are the engine, data the fuel, people steer, procedures are the service manual — remove any one and the system degrades.

questions.question: Define remote sensing, compare satellite images with aerial photographs, and discuss how remote sensing and GIS together serve population planning in South Africa, including one honest limitation.
questions.expected_answer: Remote sensing is the collection of information about the earth's surface from a distance, without physical contact, using sensors on satellites or aircraft that measure reflected solar energy — every surface returns its own signature of visible and invisible wavelengths such as infrared, which software converts into images that can reveal crop stress, soil moisture or fire heat invisible to the eye. Satellite images, from platforms like the Landsat series (imaging since 1972) and the Sentinel fleet, cover enormous areas and revisit the same ground on a fixed cycle, building time series that expose change — Theewaterskloof Dam shrinking through the Cape drought, suburbs spreading. Aerial photographs are taken from low-flying aircraft, covering small areas in fine detail; corrected orthophotos form the base of South Africa's 1:10 000 orthophoto maps. Together with GIS, the applications include: tracking informal settlement growth in metros such as Ekurhuleni and Buffalo City, where new roof clusters seen months apart become a GIS layer overlaid on water, sanitation and clinic layers to direct services; census preparation, where Statistics South Africa uses imagery to divide the country into enumeration areas so every dwelling is on an enumerator's map, with census counts becoming attribute data afterwards; disaster response, as when before-and-after images mapped the burnt neighbourhoods of the June 2017 Knysna fires while roads were closed; and food security, with infrared sensors flagging failing harvests months early. National capacity includes SANSA's Hartebeesthoek ground station and locally built satellites such as ZACube-2. The limitation: sensors count roofs, not people — no image can supply residents' ages, language or employment, so the ground census remains irreplaceable, with remote sensing and fieldwork as partners.
